title: Trees, Ensembles and Support Vector Machines
subtitle: From axis-aligned splits and bagging to maximum-margin classifiers
task: Given two measurements, predict a binary label with a flexible nonlinear boundary. Compare a single decision tree, bagged and boosted ensembles, and support vector machines on the same training, validation and test split, then choose one model using validation evidence.
motivation: The same prediction can come from very different assumptions: a tree carves the plane into rectangles, bagging averages many unstable trees, boosting corrects errors in sequence, and an SVM chooses the widest separating street. Putting them on the same data makes their inductive biases, failure modes and validation choices concrete.

stages.title: Meet the data and the split
stages.description: See why two moons need a curved boundary, inspect iris petals for a margin lesson, and reserve train / validation / test rows before fitting anything.

stages.title: Grow one tree, then average many
stages.description: Control tree depth, compare bagging with random feature selection, and read validation and out-of-bag evidence.

stages.title: Correct errors in sequence
stages.description: Fit AdaBoost and gradient boosting, tune the learning rate, and use staged validation curves to stop adding trees.

stages.title: Choose a margin and change the geometry
stages.description: Read support vectors and soft-margin C on iris petals, then compare linear, polynomial and RBF kernels on two moons and XOR.

stages.title: Compare, choose and test once
stages.description: Put all candidates on one validation table, inspect errors, freeze a choice with a written reason, and report one final test.

objectives: Explain how a decision tree uses axis-aligned splits and how depth and leaf size control overfitting.
Distinguish bagging from random forests, and interpret validation and out-of-bag evidence for ensemble size and feature randomness.
Explain how AdaBoost and gradient boosting correct previous errors, and select a learning rate and number of trees using staged validation curves.
Identify margins, support vectors and the role of C in a soft-margin SVM, and connect the geometry to hinge loss.
Compare linear, polynomial and RBF kernels, explain the effect of gamma and degree, and recognize when a kernel is needed.
Select a model on validation data, inspect its confusion matrix, and evaluate the frozen choice once on held-out test data.
prerequisites: Basic Python and NumPy, plus binary classification, accuracy, precision and recall from lecture. No previous tree, ensemble or SVM implementation is required.
outcome: An executed notebook with decision-boundary plots, validation comparisons for every model family, one inspected error case, and a justified final test result.

chapters.title: Data: Two Moons and Iris Petals
chapters.question: What makes a boundary nonlinear?
chapters.conceptTitle: Two geometric problems, one fair split
chapters.idea: A classifier learns from examples. Here each example has two measurements and a binary label; the boundary is what we want to see.
points: The `two moons` set has 600 points arranged in two interleaving crescents. No straight line separates the classes, so a flexible boundary is necessary.
The `iris petals` set uses 100 flowers from two species and two measurements: petal length and petal width. It gives a small, interpretable stage for a linear margin.
We use a stratified 60% / 20% / 20% split with seed 3612. The test rows are hidden from the browser and from editable snippets.
A model is fitted on training rows, compared on validation rows and tested once. The majority-class baseline is 50% on the balanced moon and iris splits.
notation: Two measured features for example i.
chapters.starter:
print("Moons train / validation:", X_train.shape, X_val.shape)
print("Train labels:", np.bincount(y_train.astype(int)))
print("Validation labels:", np.bincount(y_val.astype(int)))
baseline = np.zeros(len(y_val), dtype=int)
print("Always-0 validation accuracy:", metrics(y_val, baseline)["accuracy"])
print("Iris train / validation:", X_iris_train.shape[0], X_iris_val.shape[0])
print("XOR train / validation:", X_xor_train.shape[0], X_xor_val.shape[0])
chapters.experiment: Compare the two scatter plots. Why would a single straight line struggle on two moons but work better on iris petals?
chapters.activityTitle: Inspect the data and the baseline
chapters.pythonTitle: Python: shapes, splits and a baseline

chapters.title: A Single Decision Tree
chapters.question: How does one tree carve up the plane?
chapters.conceptTitle: A tree asks a sequence of yes/no questions
chapters.idea: A decision tree partitions the plane with axis-aligned splits. Each internal node tests one feature against a threshold; each leaf predicts a class.
points: Each split chooses the feature and threshold that most reduce impurity on the training rows. Gini impurity is one common criterion; entropy is another.
Depth and minimum leaf size control capacity. A deep tree can chase noisy points and produce a jagged boundary.
Training accuracy usually increases with depth. Use validation accuracy to choose a tree that generalizes.
Axis-aligned splits are interpretable, but diagonal or curved boundaries become stair-step approximations.
notation: A candidate node in the tree.
Proportion of class k among training rows reaching node t.
Gini impurity; zero means the node is pure.
chapters.starter:
for depth in (1, 2, 4, None):
    model = build_tree(depth=depth).fit(X_train, y_train)
    train = metrics(y_train, model.predict(X_train))["accuracy"]
    validation = metrics(y_val, model.predict(X_val))["accuracy"]
    print("depth", depth, "| train", round(train, 3), "| validation", round(validation, 3))
chapters.experiment: Start with depth 1. Increase depth and watch the boundary. When does training accuracy stop being a useful guide?
chapters.activityTitle: Change the tree depth and watch the boundary

chapters.title: Bagging and Random Forests
chapters.question: Why average many trees?
chapters.idea: Bagging trains trees on bootstrap samples and averages their predictions. A random forest adds random feature subsets at each split to decorrelate the trees.
points: Bagging draws rows with replacement. Each tree sees a different sample, so their errors are not identical.
A random forest also considers only a random subset of features at each split. This prevents one dominant feature from making every tree nearly the same.
Averaging reduces variance most when individual trees are strong but different. More trees stabilize predictions; gains eventually flatten.
Out-of-bag rows are omitted from a tree's bootstrap sample. Their score is an internal estimate, not a replacement for the validation split.
notation: Number of trees in the ensemble.
Averaged probability used by the ensemble.
chapters.starter:
for mode in ("bagging", "forest"):
    model = build_forest(mode=mode, n_estimators=100).fit(X_train, y_train)
    print(mode, "| OOB", round(model.oob_score_, 3),
          "| validation", round(metrics(y_val, model.predict(X_val))["accuracy"], 3))
chapters.experiment: Compare bagging and the random forest at the same number of trees. Does feature randomness change validation accuracy, and how variable is the curve?
chapters.activityTitle: Compare bagging with a random forest
chapters.pythonTitle: Python: bagging, random forest and OOB

chapters.title: Boosting: Learn from Mistakes
chapters.question: How does a sequence of weak trees become strong?
chapters.conceptTitle: Build a strong model from weak corrections
chapters.idea: Boosting fits learners sequentially. AdaBoost increases the weight of misclassified rows; gradient boosting fits each new tree to the current errors.
points: AdaBoost reweights training rows after each weak learner. Gradient boosting fits each new tree to the negative gradient of the loss.
The learning rate scales each new tree's contribution. A smaller rate often needs more trees; too many trees can still overfit.
A staged validation curve records accuracy after each added tree, so you can see when extra capacity stops helping.
Boosting focuses on hard examples, which also makes it sensitive to label noise and outliers.

Libraries such as XGBoost implement the same additive idea with additional regularization and engineering optimizations. This lesson uses scikit-learn's implementation so every example runs in the browser.
notation: The next weak learner fitted to the current errors.
Learning rate, also called the shrinkage factor.
chapters.starter:
for lr in (0.05, 0.1, 0.5):
    model = build_boosting(mode="gradient", n_estimators=100, learning_rate=lr)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    train = metrics(y_train, model.predict(X_train))["accuracy"]
    validation = metrics(y_val, model.predict(X_val))["accuracy"]
    print("learning rate", lr, "| train", round(train, 3), "| validation", round(validation, 3))
chapters.experiment: Hold the number of trees fixed and change the learning rate. Which setting reaches a good validation score with fewer trees?

chapters.title: Support Vector Machines: The Widest Street
chapters.question: Which separating line should we prefer?
chapters.conceptTitle: Among separating lines, prefer the widest street
chapters.idea: A linear SVM chooses the separating hyperplane with the largest margin. Points on the margin or inside it are support vectors; they determine the boundary.
points: The margin is the distance between the boundary and the nearest training points. Maximizing it is a geometric regularizer.
Soft-margin SVM allows violations. C trades margin width against training errors: larger C permits fewer violations and usually a narrower margin.
The hinge loss is zero beyond the margin and grows linearly for points inside it or on the wrong side.
Support vectors are the training points that matter. Moving a non-support point slightly may leave the fitted boundary unchanged.
notation: Weights and intercept of the separating line.
Slack for how far point i violates the margin.
Penalty for violations. Small C allows a wider, softer margin.
chapters.starter:
for C in (0.01, 0.1, 1, 10):
    model = build_svm(kernel="linear", C=C).fit(X_iris_train, y_iris_train)
    train = metrics(y_iris_train, model.predict(X_iris_train))["accuracy"]
    validation = metrics(y_iris_val, model.predict(X_iris_val))["accuracy"]
    print("C", C, "| support vectors", len(model.support_),
          "| train", round(train, 3), "| validation", round(validation, 3))
chapters.experiment: Move C from small to large. What happens to the margin, the number of support vectors, and validation accuracy?
chapters.pythonTitle: Python: support vectors and the C setting

chapters.title: Kernels: Change the Geometry
chapters.question: What if a straight line cannot separate the classes?
chapters.conceptTitle: Kernels let a linear boundary act in a richer space
chapters.idea: A kernel computes an inner product in a transformed feature space without explicitly building that space. Polynomial and RBF kernels produce curved boundaries in the original plane.
points: Linear: `K(x,z)=x·z`. Polynomial: `K(x,z)=(γ x·z+r)^d`. RBF: `K(x,z)=exp(-γ||x-z||²)`.
Gamma controls the reach of each point: small gamma gives smooth, broad boundaries; large gamma gives local, wiggly ones.
The kernel trick replaces dot products; the SVM still solves the same convex optimization problem.
XOR has no useful linear split. A linear SVM fails; an RBF kernel can separate the quadrants.
notation: RBF reach: larger values make each point's influence more local.
Polynomial degree: larger values add higher-order interactions.
chapters.starter:
for kernel in ("linear", "poly", "rbf"):
    model = build_svm(kernel=kernel, C=1, gamma=1, degree=3)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    validation = metrics(y_val, model.predict(X_val))["accuracy"]
    print(kernel, "| support vectors", len(model.support_),
          "| validation", round(validation, 3))
for kernel in ("linear", "rbf"):
    model = build_svm(kernel=kernel, C=1, gamma=1).fit(X_xor_train, y_xor_train)
    print("XOR", kernel, "| validation", round(metrics(y_xor_val, model.predict(X_xor_val))["accuracy"], 3))
chapters.experiment: Switch between moons and XOR. Which kernel can bend enough for each dataset? What does a very large gamma do?
chapters.activityTitle: Compare kernels on two moons and XOR
chapters.pythonTitle: Python: linear, polynomial and RBF kernels

chapters.title: Compare, Choose, Test
chapters.question: Which model deserves the final test?
chapters.idea: Each family has a different inductive bias. Compare their validation performance and errors, choose one, and evaluate it once on the test split.
points: Every candidate uses the same training rows and the same validation rows. Changing the split changes the comparison.
Validation accuracy is a starting point. Inspect the confusion matrix and individual errors before choosing.
A more flexible model can win on training data and lose on validation. The test set does not help you choose.
Record a reason before the final test. Once evaluated, the test decision is frozen.
notation: One candidate model and its fitted settings.
The candidate selected before seeing test results.
chapters.starter:
rows = compare_models()["rows"]
for row in rows:
    print(row["name"], "| validation", round(row["validation"]["accuracy"], 3))
best = max(rows, key=lambda row: row["validation"]["accuracy"])
print("Selected on validation:", best["name"])
print("Write a reason before running the final test cell.")
